title: Design and Extend Shared Helpers
readerIntent: Create a stable helper without hiding dependencies or ownership.
priorKnowledge: Know all current and intended consumers.
summary: A shared helper has explicit inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, performance, security, compatibility, consumers, and override rules.

sections.heading: Implementation sequence
items: Search for an existing helper and owning capability.
Prove several framework consumers and no clearer owner before using nCommon.
Prefer a pure deterministic function; pass required context explicitly.
Avoid network, filesystem, provider, database, secret, or mutable-global behavior in a general utility.
Document compatibility and layer overrides; never monkey-patch globals.
Test invalid input, boundaries, error cause propagation, concurrency where relevant, and all critical consumers.

sections.heading: Design the contract
items: Name the owning capability and consumers.
Define accepted types, output, mutation, null behavior, and errors.
Document time and space complexity and input bounds.
Make locale, time zone, encoding, and comparison choices explicit.
Decide whether extension is supported or a breaking change requires a new helper.

sections.heading: Example: friendly description
paragraphs: A presentation helper can truncate a description to five words and preserve the full text for a tooltip. It receives text and a word limit and returns deterministic display data.
The helper does not search records, authorize visibility, or choose which description field is safe; those decisions remain with schema metadata and backend contracts.

sections.heading: Security and performance
items: Never add secret-bearing convenience serialization or logging.
Keep high-volume helpers bounded and allocation-aware.
Preserve original safe cause, correlation, module, tenant, and execution layer.
Measure widely used helpers before adding expensive abstraction.

sections.heading: Failure and compatibility tests
items: Undefined, null, empty, wrong-type, Unicode, and very large input.
Minimum, maximum, truncation, ordering, and immutability boundaries.
Malicious object keys, unsafe formats, and log injection.
Concurrent use with no shared mutable state.
Performance under expected high-volume use.
All critical current consumers before and after the change.

sections.heading: When to refactor into a service
paragraphs: Move behavior out of a utility when it needs injected configuration, cache, database, filesystem, network, provider choice, authorization, tenant context, metrics lifecycle, or customer-specific override.
Preserve a small pure helper inside the service only when it still has independent mechanical value.
